claims.text: Solidified, single-phase FeNiCrMn has low stacking-fault energy.
Stacking-fault energy governs the dynamic mechanical response of solidified, single-phase FeNiCrMn.
Stacking-fault energy controls a temperature- and strain-rate-dependent transition from dislocation slip to deformation twinning.
The onset and amount of deformation twinning determine yield strength under dynamic loading.
The onset and amount of deformation twinning determine work-hardening rate under dynamic loading.
The onset and amount of deformation twinning determine ductility under dynamic loading.
Lower temperatures and higher strain rates promote deformation twinning in FeNiCrMn by causing the critical resolved shear stress for twinning to be exceeded.
The critical resolved shear stress for twinning is related to stacking-fault energy.
Deformation twinning enhances work hardening in FeNiCrMn.
Deformation twinning contributes to ductility in FeNiCrMn.
At higher temperatures and lower strain rates, dislocation slip dominates deformation.
Slip-dominated deformation at higher temperatures and lower strain rates produces lower strength.
Slip-dominated deformation at higher temperatures and lower strain rates produces reduced work hardening.
Conditions producing at least 10 vol% deformation twins will exhibit higher yield strength than conditions producing less than 5 vol% twins.
Conditions producing at least 10 vol% deformation twins will exhibit higher work-hardening rates than conditions producing less than 5 vol% twins.
Ductility will remain comparable or become slightly higher under twin-active conditions.
The proposed hypothesis applies to homogenized, single-phase FCC FeNiCrMn with a grain size of 20–100 µm over 77–500 K and strain rates of 10^-3–10^4 s^-1.
A systematic tensile-testing study will vary temperature and strain rate and quantify deformation-twin volume fraction using EBSD or high-energy X-ray diffraction.
A twin volume fraction below 5 vol% under every tested condition would falsify the hypothesis.
A lack of positive correlation between measured twin fraction and variations in yield strength and work-hardening rate would falsify the hypothesis.
